title: Ciné-dancing, Aubette, Strasbourg
lede: Van Doesburg’s cinema and dance hall of 1926–1928, reconstructed: walls and ceiling covered with large colored squares set on the diagonal.
summary: Tilted red, yellow, blue, green, and gray squares in relief across walls and ceiling. Theo van Doesburg, 1926–1928, reconstructed.
made: 1926–1928; covered over in 1938; reconstructed in the 1990s and 2000s

evidence.note: Inspected a photograph of the reconstructed room by the Commons user Clostridium ([File:Aubette cine dancing doesburg.JPG](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Aubette_cine_dancing_doesburg.JPG), 1024 × 768 px, viewed at 960 px). The photograph shows the present reconstruction, not the 1928 surfaces.

styles.note: Partial fit, Elementarism: flat primaries, gray, and white in rectangular panels, but the main structure is diagonal, the branch the style record treats as related, not core.

context: Theo van Doesburg, Sophie Taeuber-Arp, and Jean Arp decorated the Aubette entertainment complex on Place Kléber in 1926–1928. Van Doesburg did two cafés and two dance halls. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aubette_(building)).

The decorations were covered over in 1938. The cinema and staircase became historic monuments in 1985, and renovations were completed in 1994 and 2006. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aubette_(building)).
Wikipedia describes the scheme as an orthogonal composition in primary colors; the photograph shows the panels turned 45°, so that description does not match this room.
observed: Raised bands divide the walls and ceiling into large squares turned 45°, so every edge runs on the diagonal.
The squares are painted red, yellow, dark blue, green, gray, and off-white; two red panels sit on the ceiling.
A metal balcony and stair cross the left wall; a straight rail hung from the ceiling carries a row of conical metal lamps.
Low booths with white panels edged in black stand on a blue floor.
The warm lighting of the photograph shifts the whites and yellows toward cream.
interpretation: The room is van Doesburg’s counter-composition in space: the same flat colored planes as neoplasticism, turned against the orthogonal architecture. It is the clearest built example of the diagonal that divided him from Mondrian.
Use it as a contrast case for the fingerprint: a diagonal grid in the De Stijl palette should read as Elementarism.
borrow: For a single dramatic room or section, rotate a De Stijl grid 45° against an orthogonal frame, and keep everything else square.

images.alt: Interior of a large hall whose walls and ceiling are divided into big squares turned 45°, painted red, yellow, dark blue, green, and gray; a metal balcony and stair, a row of hanging conical lamps, and low white booths on a blue floor.
images.caption: Ciné-dancing of the Aubette, Strasbourg, designed by Theo van Doesburg in 1926–1928, as reconstructed. Photograph by Clostridium on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Aubette_cine_dancing_doesburg.JPG), released into the public domain.

rights.statement: The photographer released the photograph into the public domain (PD-self on Commons). The design is by Theo van Doesburg, who died in 1931, so it is public domain in France and the Netherlands; interiors finished in 1928 are not protected in the United States. The reconstruction copies his design and adds no new authorship that this record relies on.
